lecture.title: MIT 6.004 S17 — Chapter 1: Basics of Information

notes.summary: Computation Structures begins where the machine begins: information itself. Bits measure surprise — entropy quantifies it — and encoding (like binary numbers) lets us transmit information reliably. Error detection and correction (parity, Hamming) close the chapter. The 6.191 course at MIT (its successor, live at 6191.mit.edu/fall26) covers the same arc this term.
notes.focus: Compute the entropy of a biased coin for p = 0.5, 0.9, 0.99 and plot it. Seeing entropy collapse as certainty rises is the whole chapter in one graph.

lecture.title: MIT 6.004 S17 — Chapter 2: The Digital Abstraction

notes.summary: The magic trick of digital systems: real voltages are messy analogs, but by declaring voltage ranges as '0' and '1' with a forbidden gap, noise gets squeezed out at every stage. The voltage discipline and the noise margins are the contract that makes digital logic possible — and combinational devices are defined as digital gates with no memory.
notes.focus: Draw the voltage transfer curve of a buffer and mark VIL, VIH, VOL, VOH. The gaps between them are the noise immunity you rely on for every gate.

notes.summary: Transistors as voltage-controlled switches: nMOS pulls low, pMOS pulls high, and the CMOS recipe — pull-up network of pMOS, complementary pull-down of nMOS — builds any inverting gate. You learn to synthesize NAND/NOR gates from Boolean expressions and see why CMOS draws power mostly on switching.
notes.focus: Draw the transistor schematic for a 2-input NAND from the recipe, then check: is the pull-down exactly complementary to the pull-up? It must be.

lecture.title: MIT 6.004 S17 — Chapter 4: Gates & Boolean logic

notes.summary: Boolean algebra as the simplification calculus: truth tables to expressions to sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms, with axioms and theorems doing the reduction. Then the move from theory to hardware: gates as physical devices with propagation delays — logic that costs time.
notes.focus: Simplify one Boolean expression two ways — algebraically and via truth table — and confirm they agree. Then compute the propagation delay of your circuit from its depth.

notes.summary: Memory enters the machine: latches sample the input while enabled; edge-triggered D registers capture on clock edges. Timing discipline — setup, hold, and the clock period budget — is the price of state. This is where hardware becomes sequential, and the clock period becomes the speed limit of everything.
notes.focus: Draw the timing budget for a register-to-register path. If you can explain why the clock period must exceed tPD + tSETUP, sequential timing holds no mysteries.

notes.summary: FSMs tame time: state registers hold history, combinational logic computes the next state and outputs. You design Moore vs Mealy machines from specifications, and meet the course's famous roboant — a line-following robot whose brain is an FSM you can fully analyze. This is the same machine model CS188 will borrow for MDPs.
notes.focus: Design an FSM for a sequence detector (e.g., recognize 101) with a full transition table, then trace it through the input to prove it works.

notes.summary: Pipelining divides a slow stage chain into balanced shorter stages: throughput rises even though single-item latency doesn't. Register overhead per stage, stage balancing, and the classic K-stage speedup formula appear here — the same economics that drive CPU pipelines and GPU shader stages in 6.1810's world.
notes.focus: Compute the throughput of a 3-stage pipeline with register overhead, then find the k that maximizes it. The calculus is trivial and the insight is universal.

notes.summary: Building the machine's arithmetic: ripple-carry adders are slow, carry-lookahead buys speed with logic, carry-select trades area. Fixed-point representations (two's complement!) let these circuits subtract and detect overflow. The programmable datapath — an ALU plus registers and a control input — is the skeleton of every computer.
notes.focus: Convert a few numbers to two's complement by hand and add a negative to a positive. When you can predict overflow on paper, the arithmetic unit is demystified.

lessons.title: The von Neumann Model and the Beta ISA

notes.summary: The stored-program computer: instructions live in memory, the Beta ISA is the course's clean 32-bit RISC design, and its fetch-execute cycle is microcoded control. Every program you have ever run is this loop. You'll write Beta assembly next and watch the exact instructions a compiler would emit.
concepts: The Beta registers and instruction format
notes.focus: Trace one load instruction through fetch, decode, and execute on the Beta datapath diagram. One instruction, fully traced, is worth a hundred skimmed.

notes.summary: Programming the machine: Beta assembly for arithmetic, control flow, and procedure calls. Activation records — the stack frame of saved registers, locals, and the return address — make recursion possible at the hardware level. The compiler chapters (11) translate expressions into exactly the instructions you write by hand here.
notes.focus: Hand-assemble a recursive factorial into Beta assembly with correct stack frames. Then trace the stack growing and shrinking — recursion you can SEE.

notes.summary: The gap between CPU speed and memory speed is bridged by hierarchy: registers, SRAM caches, DRAM, disk. Direct-mapped caches use address bits for index and tag; LRU approximations and write policies tune hit rates. The classic analysis — average access time as a weighted hit/miss mix — applies to every cache in every system you will ever profile.
notes.focus: For a given address stream and cache geometry, compute the hit rate by hand. Draw the address split (tag|index|offset) first — the rest follows mechanically.

notes.summary: Checkpoint from bits to the von Neumann machine: digital abstraction, CMOS, Boolean simplification, sequential timing, FSMs, pipelining, and datapaths. The exam tests design judgment — choosing representations and circuits for a spec — so drill the design problems, not just exercises.
notes.focus: Redo the weakest chapter's design problem from a blank page. 6.004 exams reward clean derivations over clever guesses.

lessons.title: Final: Virtual Memory and the OS Interface

notes.summary: The course closes with virtual memory (page maps, TLBs, protection) and the interrupt-driven handoff to operating systems — exactly where 6.1810 picks up next term with xv6. Pipeline hazards (the video) recap why hardware and compilers co-evolve. From entropy to a virtual machine: you have now built the whole conceptual machine stack.
notes.focus: Translate one virtual address through a 2-level page table by hand. When that works, the OS's memory tricks in 6.1810 will feel like old friends.
